name: The Harlow Experiments
statement: Infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother that gave no food over a wire one that did, showing comfort matters more than feeding.
statementAccent: showing comfort matters more than feeding
meaning: The Harlow experiments were a series of studies on attachment and social development conducted by the psychologist Harry Harlow at the University of Wisconsin from the 1950s into the 1960s, using infant rhesus monkeys separated from their mothers. In the most famous studies, an infant monkey was raised with two artificial surrogate mothers: one made of bare wire that dispensed milk from a bottle, and one covered in soft cloth that gave no food. Contrary to the then-dominant view that infants bond to their mothers mainly because mothers provide food, the young monkeys spent most of their time clinging to the soft cloth mother and went to the wire mother only briefly to feed, returning to the cloth mother for comfort, especially when frightened. Harlow concluded that contact comfort, the reassurance of soft physical contact, was more important than feeding in forming attachment. His later and far more disturbing studies of maternal and social deprivation, in which monkeys were reared in isolation, showed severe and lasting emotional and social damage. The experiments were highly influential for attachment theory but are also notorious for their cruelty to the animals.
mechanism: In the surrogate-mother studies, newborn rhesus monkeys were separated from their real mothers and raised in cages containing two inanimate surrogates. One surrogate was constructed of wire mesh and fitted with a bottle so it provided milk; the other was wrapped in soft terry cloth but provided no food. Harlow measured how much time the infants spent on each surrogate and how they behaved under stress. The monkeys overwhelmingly preferred the cloth mother, clinging to it for most of the day and using it as a secure base, approaching the wire mother only to nurse and then returning to the cloth one. When a frightening object was introduced, the infants ran to the cloth mother for comfort, and those with only a wire mother were more disturbed. This directly contradicted the cupboard-love theory that attachment forms simply because the caregiver supplies food, showing instead that contact comfort drives bonding. In the deprivation studies, monkeys reared in total or partial isolation, sometimes in an apparatus Harlow grimly called the pit of despair, developed profound and often irreversible disturbances, becoming withdrawn, self-harming, and unable to socialize or parent normally, demonstrating the lasting damage of early social and maternal deprivation.

examples.text: Infant monkeys clung to the soft cloth surrogate that gave no milk and visited the wire, milk-giving surrogate only briefly to feed.

whyItMatters: The Harlow experiments transformed the understanding of love, attachment, and early development by overturning the prevailing view that infants bond to caregivers chiefly because they are fed. By showing that infant monkeys preferred a soft, comforting surrogate that gave no food over a wire one that did, Harlow demonstrated that contact comfort is central to attachment, a finding that supported and enriched attachment theory, associated with John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, and reshaped thinking about the emotional needs of infants. His deprivation studies, however harrowing, revealed the profound and lasting damage caused by early social and maternal isolation, informing views on institutional care, orphanages, neglect, and the importance of nurturing contact in child-rearing. At the same time, the experiments are a central example in debates over research ethics and animal welfare, because the suffering deliberately inflicted on the monkeys was severe, and they helped galvanize the animal-rights movement. The Harlow experiments thus matter both for their lasting scientific contribution to the psychology of attachment and as a stark ethical cautionary tale.

limits: The Harlow experiments are limited and troubling in several ways. They were conducted on rhesus monkeys, so generalizing directly to human attachment requires caution, though the parallels are suggestive. Above all, they involved deliberate and severe cruelty, separating infants from mothers and rearing some in prolonged isolation that caused profound suffering, which would be ethically indefensible today and stands as a major criticism of the work. The surrogate studies simplify attachment to two artificial figures and cannot capture the full complexity of a real caregiving relationship. The deprivation findings, while striking, come from extreme and artificial conditions. So the Harlow experiments robustly established that contact comfort is central to attachment and that early deprivation is deeply harmful, understood as findings from animal studies obtained through ethically indefensible cruelty and generalized to humans with care.
misreadings: The Harlow experiments do not show that feeding is irrelevant to caregiving; they show that contact comfort, not feeding alone, drives attachment, overturning the idea that infants bond simply because they are fed. The findings come from monkeys, so they inform but do not by themselves prove claims about human children. And the studies were not benign observation but involved deliberate, severe cruelty, so treating feeding as unimportant, the monkey results as automatically human, or the methods as ethically acceptable, misreads influential but deeply troubling animal experiments on attachment.
origin: A series of attachment studies by the psychologist Harry Harlow at the University of Wisconsin from the 1950s into the 1960s, using infant rhesus monkeys and surrogate mothers; influential for attachment theory and notorious for their cruelty.
